10030-the-life-of-hon-william-f-cody-kno:
William F. Cody, known as Buffalo Bill, the famous hunter, scout, and guide, told his own life in this 1879 autobiography, dedicated to General Philip H. Sheridan. Cody's portrait, signed yours sincerely, fronts the book.

His narrative, the introduction says, reads more like romance than reality, though no literary excellence is claimed for it. Its merit lies in firsthand value for the records of western frontier history. Readers get Cody's West as he wished it remembered: hunts, scouts, guides, and the wide plains before settlement closed them forever. It is the showman's own version of a life already becoming legend.
10738-mahomet-founder-of-islam:
G. M. Draycott's Mahomet, Founder of Islam tells the life of Muhammad from birthplace and childhood through strife, meditation, and inspiration. Chapters follow his flight to Medina, the consolidation of power, the battles of Bedr and Ohod, the war of the ditch, pilgrimages, and the triumphal entry into Mecca. A final chapter traces the genesis of Islam itself.

Draycott writes a straightforward narrative life, quoting Anatole France on men of action whose genius gathers on a single point. The book suits readers seeking a compact, readable account of the Prophet's career. It offers the main events in order, without deep theological argument.
1113-a-midsummer-night-s-dream:
Four young Athenians flee to a moonlit wood, where Oberon and Titania, king and queen of the fairies, quarrel over a changeling boy, and Puck's love juice sets every heart awry. William Shakespeare's comedy weaves their tangles with a troupe of rude mechanicals rehearsing a play for the duke's wedding.

Bottom the weaver, turned into an ass and doted on by Titania, steals the comedy, while the lovers wake unsure what was dream and what was real. The play ends in weddings and a famous farewell from Puck. It remains the most magical of Shakespeare's comedies.
11198-christianity-and-islam:
C. H. Becker, professor of Oriental history at Hamburg's Colonial Institute, wrote this 1909 study of Christianity and Islam, translated by Rev. H. J. Chaytor of Plymouth College. Becker warns that any comparison must state its purpose: the missionary seeks mission use, while the church-minded Christian seeks scientific proof of his own religion's superiority.

Contents trace Christianity and the rise of Islam, Muhammed and his peers, Christian influence on Muhammed, Christians under Muhammedan rule, medieval metaphysics shared by both faiths, asceticism, clerical classes, marriage, immortality, ritual. Traditions quoted include the saying that the worst use of money is to build, and that pious caliphs sat on clay thrones. Becker's book offers a scholarly, comparative history of two faiths.
1158-penrod-and-sam:
Booth Tarkington follows Penrod Schofield and his friend Sam Williams through a summer of boyhood mischief in a Midwestern town: circuses, dogs, secret societies, and scrapes with grown-ups. Penrod, twelve and earnest, means well and lands in trouble all the same.

Tarkington writes boys with humor and a kind eye, never talking down to them. The episodes are short, funny, and true to how children plot and dream. The book, a sequel to Penrod, charmed a generation, and it still reads as a classic of American boyhood. Tarkington's boys feel true, and the summer episodes still make readers laugh.
11640-love-and-mr-lewisham:
H. G. Wells follows Mr. Lewisham from his studies as an assistant master to a life pulled between career and love. The opening chapter, the book notes, does not concern itself with love, since that antagonist does not appear until chapter three.

Chapters carry Lewisham through a wonderful discovery, raised eyebrows, a scandalous ramble, and a reckoning. Alice Heydinger, Mr. Lagune, and the Friends of Progress enter his circle. At last the career is suspended, then resumed in a new form. The novel asks what a young man owes ambition, and what he owes his heart.
12322-poetical-works-of-edmund-waller-an:
The Reverend George Gilfillan edited this volume of Edmund Waller and Sir John Denham poetical works in 1857, with memoir and dissertation. Waller, a courtier poet of the seventeenth century, and Denham, author of Cooper Hill, represent the polished verse that preceded Dryden.

Gilfillan memoir notes that poets lives are seldom interesting in outward events, but rich in inner development. Poems include Waller smooth lyrics and Denham topographical verse, with lines on seas forced from course by avarice and banks decayed. The edition pairs the poems with critical comment in Gilfillan earnest Victorian manner. For students of English verse, the volume marks the turn from metaphysical wit to Augustan clarity.
13754-evesham:
Edmund H. New wrote and illustrated this 1904 portrait of Evesham, a storied town in Worcestershire. He draws on George May's 1845 history and on Oswald Knapp's articles from monastic chronicles in the Evesham Journal. Chapters follow the abbey, the bridge, and the town's streets through history. Illustrations by New himself picture old buildings and views.

New argues that such towns teach what no history book alone can tell. He praises the spirit of past builders and urges readers to match it. The book mixes antiquarian detail with affection for place. It suits walkers, local historians, and lovers of English towns. Evesham stands as a gentle example of early topographical writing.
13811-peter-stuyvesant-the-last-dutch-go:
John S. C. Abbott wrote this popular life of Peter Stuyvesant, last Dutch governor of New Amsterdam. The book begins with Hudson's voyage and the founding of the colony. It follows trade, land disputes, and quarrels with English neighbours. Stuyvesant, stern and one-legged after war wounds, rules with a firm hand.

Abbott praises Stuyvesant's energy while noting his clashes with colonists and clergy. Chapters cover Manhattan's growth, the fur trade, and the trail that became Broadway. The surrender to England in 1664 closes the Dutch period. Abbott's style is plain and anecdotal, aimed at general readers. The life gives a clear entry to early New York history.
14064-mohammed-the-prophet-of-islam:
H. E. E. Hayes wrote this popular essay on Mohammed for readers curious about Islam and mission work among Muslims. Sold cheaply from Hythe House in Kent, it opens with the Muslim creed and points readers to a quarterly review of missions in Muslim lands. Pagan Arabia frames the story: idols hollow, thoughtful men uneasy, and Jews and Christians settled in the country offering other views.

Hayes follows Mohammed from uncertainty to leadership, then judges him sternly. Early friendship with Jews turns, in his account, to harsh injustice. At Medina, refugees outgrow charity, so raids on wealthy Meccan caravans supply support, even in sacred months once held peaceful. Generosity in want earns praise, but revelations that bless new gains draw blame. The essay reads today as a missionary-era portrait: clear, partisan, and useful for studying how Britain once explained Islam to itself.
14419-grammatical-sketch-of-the-heve-lan:
Buckingham Smith translated this 1861 grammatical sketch of Heve, the language of the Eudeve people of Sonora in northern Mexico, from an unpublished Spanish manuscript. It appeared in Shea's Library of American Linguistics.

A short historical notice places the Eudeve in the Sonora region under New Spain, then the grammar sets out pronouns, cases, and verb forms with examples. Personal pronouns shift shape by person and number, and the tables show a system quite unlike Spanish. The sketch preserves a now-vanished language in brief but careful form, useful to linguists and historians.
14735-political-thought-in-england-from-:
Harold J. Laski traces English political thought from Locke to Bentham in a compact volume for the Home University Library, published in 1920. He owes much, he notes, to Leslie Stephen's history of eighteenth-century English thought, and digs among original texts rather than summaries.

Chapters move from the principles of the Revolution and church and state, through an era of stagnation and signs of change, to Burke and the foundations of economic liberalism. Locke's contract, Burke's tradition and Bentham's utility emerge as answers to their own times. Laski's book is a clear student guide to how English ideas about power, rights and markets took modern shape.
15001-the-sources-and-analogues-of-a-mid:
Frank Sidgwick compiles sources and analogues of A Midsummer Night's Dream. It was published by Duffield in New York and Chatto in London in 1908. Its Paulin Paris epigraph praises closing modern romances to study fine works of ancestors' minds, manners and beliefs.

An introduction, main sentimental plot, grotesque plot and fairy plot follow, with Oberon's vision, illustrative texts, notes and index. Sidgwick traces Shakespeare's play to earlier tales, romances and folklore, showing how Athens, rude mechanicals and fairies came together. The volume remains a useful source study for students who want to see a Shakespeare play grow from its materials.
1514-a-midsummer-night-s-dream:
On the eve of Theseus's wedding in Athens, four young lovers flee to a wood where fairies quarrel over a changeling boy. Oberon and Titania, king and queen of fairyland, cross wills, Puck's love juice misfires, and Bottom the weaver wakes with an ass's head to become Titania's beloved.

By dawn the lovers are sorted, the fairies are reconciled, and rude mechanicals stage Pyramus and Thisbe for the wedding feast. Shakespeare's comedy blends court, wood, and stage with effortless grace. It is the most beloved of his early comedies, and a perfect introduction to his magic.
154-the-rise-of-silas-lapham:
Silas Lapham made a fortune in mineral paint and wants Boston society to take him seriously. William Dean Howells's Rise of Silas Lapham opens with a journalist interviewing the blunt businessman for a series on solid men. Lapham's rise, and his moral fall and recovery, drive the novel.

His daughters, his wife Persis, and the Corey family test his manners and his conscience. A business partner's ruin forces Lapham to choose between wealth and honor. Howells uses the choice to study American success with gentle irony. The novel became a classic of literary realism.
16005-jane-sinclair-or-the-fawn-of-sprin:
William Carleton's Irish tale centers on Jane Sinclair, known far and wide as the Fawn of Springvale for her beauty and grace. Her story moves among family, neighbors, and suitors in the Irish countryside, with Charles Osborne close to her fate. Carleton writes in the warm, moral style of his other Irish sketches and novels, mixing homely detail with strong feeling.

The closing pages turn to loss: Jane's funeral train reaches the grave just as another funeral approaches, that of Charles Osborne himself. An old man who loved her sinks into grief he cannot shake, despite prayer, reading, and the comfort of his family. The book leaves readers with a tender, sad portrait of love, death, and mourning in rural Ireland.
16008-ellen-duncan-and-the-proctor-s-dau:
Two Irish tales by William Carleton, Ellen Duncan and The Proctor's Daughter, in his collected works. Ellen Duncan opens with grief so deep that friendship and sympathy cannot soothe it. Ellen weeps silently in her lone cottage on the borders of Clare, then in a frightful state of anarchy and confusion. Her husband Owen lives in the cabin where he was born.

Owen succeeded to the cabin and a few acres on his father's death, and the pair had not long been married. Never were husband and wife more loving, Carleton implies, before trouble struck. The Proctor's Daughter joins Ellen's tale as a second Irish sorrow. The volume shows Carleton at his most tender: love, loss, and a troubled county.
1611-seventeen-a-tale-of-youth-and-summe:
Booth Tarkington's Seventeen follows William Baxter, a boy of seventeen in a summer of first love, as he moons over a visiting girl, borrows his father's evening clothes. Suffers the torments of the painful age. His little sister Jane, with big ears for his secrets, adds comedy at every turn.

Through garden parties, a dog named Clematis, and sorrows within a boiler, Tarkington captures adolescence with affectionate accuracy. The novel is funny without cruelty. Seventeen remains a classic American portrait of youth, and a warm, nostalgic read for grown-ups who remember being seventeen.
17125-more-william:
Richmal Crompton's More William, first issued in December 1922 and reprinted through 1924, gathers fourteen tales of William Brown and his outlaws. A busy Christmas Day opens the set, with presents, turkey, and too many relations. Rice mould, a burglar, a knight at arms, a ghost, a May king, a revenge, a smuggler, and a Christmas Eve follow, all pictured by Thomas Henry.

William's schemes, his scorn for grown-up ways, and his loyal gang drive each story. Crompton writes with brisk humor and a sharp ear for boy talk. Children and nostalgic adults alike will enjoy this classic set, where every good plan goes gloriously, hilariously wrong.
17213-the-future-of-islam:
Wilfrid Scawen Blunt's 1882 essays, first printed in the Fortnightly Review in 1881, ask what lies ahead for the Muslim world. Chapters give a census of that world and the Haj, the modern question of the caliphate, Mecca as true metropolis, a Muslim reformation, and England's interest in Islam. Blunt wrote in haste as France moved in Tunis and Egypt stirred for reform.

He urges Britain to lead rather than be led by a wave of religious energy sweeping east, and he pleads for knowledge before choice. The essays are bold, dated, and still sharp on empire and faith. Readers of Victorian views of Islam will find a frank, opinionated book from a critic of his own country's policy.
1743-twelve-stories-and-a-dream:
H. G. Wells gathers twelve stories and a dream in this volume, ranging from the comic to the uncanny. Filmer invents a flying machine, a magic shop sells wonders with a price, spiders fill a valley, and Mr. Skelmersdale spends a night in fairyland and comes back changed. A new accelerator speeds the body, and an inexperienced ghost learns his trade.

Wells's range is the point: satire, horror, and speculation sit side by side, and each tale turns on one bold idea followed through to its end. Readers who know his novels will enjoy the shorter form, where a single notion — a shop, a drug, a valley — is enough to carry a whole story.
17799-yorkshire-ditties-second-series-to:
John Hartley wrote these Yorkshire Ditties, with a second series joined to the cream of his wit and humor, printed at Wakefield and London. Hartley, born in 1839 and dead by 1915, wrote in broad Yorkshire speech, and his publishers vow the book will please lovers of their native twang.

Pieces include Th' Better Part, My Grandfather's Days, Heart Broken, To a Daisy, and An Old Man's Christmas Morning. The verse is homely, funny, and warm, full of farm folk, chapel, and fireside talk. Readers who like dialect verse will enjoy the sound of Yorkshire in print, though the spelling asks for a slow, aloud read.
18664-the-hills-of-hingham:
Dallas Lore Sharp published this book of essays at Boston and New York in 1916, with pictures. It centers on his family's hill home at Hingham, Massachusetts, a compromise between town life and the wild Arden of youth. Sharp jokes that Hingham's hills need no great height to feel like hills, and that his household buys olives but grows its own apples, peaches, and melons.

Chapters cover the open fire, the ice crop, seed catalogues, spring ploughing, beans, pigs, leafing, and the Christmas tree, with a pilgrim from Dubuque and a return to town. Sharp writes with humor and warmth about country living near Boston. The book suits readers who love nature essays.
19209-the-andes-and-the-amazon-or-across:
James Orton, professor of natural history at Vassar, wrote this 1870 travel and science book, The Andes and the Amazon, across the continent of South America. With a new map of equatorial America and many pictures, it joins exploration, natural history, and peoples of the Amazon basin. Orton entered the work in 1869.

Palms on the middle Amazon front the book, while chapters cross high Andes, descend to tropical rivers, and note plants, animals, and native life. The tone is that of a learned Victorian traveller. Readers get a classic South American journey, rich in nature and adventure.
19746-the-colonel-s-dream:
Charles W. Chesnutt wrote this novel of the post-war South, first out from a New York press in the early nineteen hundreds. A colonel returns to a southern town with a dream of progress, seeking to bring enlightenment to vexed problems of race, work, and rule.

Chesnutt dedicates the book to all who labor, near or far, for that good end, and warns that its themes, love, faith, hope, and sorrow, are never new, only ever urgent. The novel is a sober, humane plea from one of America's first major Black novelists.
19874-bubbles-of-the-foam:
Bubbles of the Foam offers Eastern tales translated from an original manuscript. Its voices include the god Maheshwara roaming with Parwati in his arms. One speaker calls himself rival and reflection of the universe. He has bones instead of stars, wasted skeletons instead of a Milky Way. The tales wear a dreamlike, cosmic dress. F. W. Bain translated such Hindu stories for English readers.

Bain presented his tales as renderings from Sanskrit manuscripts. Readers loved their strange, perfumed philosophy. Life, death, and gods trade speeches in fleeting scenes. The foam of the title is existence itself, brief and bright. Bain's authenticity was debated even then. The stories endure as English literary curiosities regardless.
20660-the-faith-of-islam:
The Faith of Islam is a study of Muslim belief and practice written for English readers. Its author explains his plan at the start. The book does not set out to tell the life of Muhammad, or the wide and rapid spread of the system he founded.

Instead it opens the faith itself: its creed, prayers, fasts, law, and sects. Such handbooks served missionaries, officials, and travelers in lands under Muslim rule. The book's strength is its order. Doctrine by doctrine, it shows what Muslims are taught to believe and do. It uses the terms of the faith's own scholars, as far as the writer could reach them.
20935-the-substance-of-a-dream:
A snowdrift hump, missed by a drowsy mind, sparks a wild urge to roll in The Substance of a Dream. Legs fly skyward as the dreamer tumbles side to side in the snow. F. W. Bain frames his tale as turned from a Sanskrit source manuscript.

Bain wrote sly, jewel-like tales in an Indian mould for English readers. Dreams, gods, love, and fate twist through his brief, rich plots. His claim of old manuscripts was part of the artful game. Readers get tales that feel at once ancient and arch, small in size yet heavy with charm and craft.
2191-boy-scouts-in-mexico-or-on-guard-wi:
G. Harvey Ralphson sends a patrol of Boy Scouts across the border into Mexico, where a planned vacation turns into a test of pluck and teamwork. The boys use signals, codes, and woodcraft as they follow a trail of suspects, bears, and strange disappearances through mountain country. Each chapter ends with a fresh puzzle for the patrol to solve.

The story teaches scouting skills by putting them to work, from tracking to keeping cool under threat. Friendship and duty to the flag run through the adventure without slowing it down. Young readers get a fast, old-fashioned tale of boys proving themselves far from home.
22134-gathering-jewels-the-secret-of-a-b:
Gathering Jewels, printed in 1887, is a memorial volume subtitled The Secret of a Beautiful Life. James Knowles compiled it in memory of a beloved woman of his family. He argues that such memoirs should wait until grief has softened, but not so long that memories fade. The book gathers letters, recollections, and the record of a Christian life at home.

Friends' impressions stand beside the editor's own account. The "jewels" of the title are the virtues the life displayed, gathered one by one. Memorial volumes filled Victorian shelves, keeping the dead present in the parlour. This one shows the genre's tenderness and its faith that a quiet life deserved print.
23043-two-gentlemen-of-verona-the-works-:
Valentine lectures Proteus in Two Gentlemen of Verona, printed here from the Cambridge Shakespeare. Cease to persuade, my loving Proteus, he says. Home-keeping youth have ever homely wits. Love chains Proteus at home, Valentine says. Otherwise he would beg his friend's company for a tour of the world's wonders abroad.

The play follows two friends divided by love for the same woman, with disguise, exile, and a very patient heroine in Julia. It is early Shakespeare, quick, musical, and a little cruel at the end. The Cambridge text brings the editors' collation to the page, letting readers see the play as nineteenth-century scholarship rebuilt it. Friendship, in this comedy, survives things friendship should not.
24107-the-new-world-of-islam:
Lothrop Stoddard published this survey of the Islamic world in London in 1922, with a map of Muslim lands. He traces the fall of the old Islamic order. Forces remaking it include a religious revival, pan-Islamism, the press of Western power, and new waves of political, national, economic, and social change. A chapter treats nationalism in India, and a closing chapter weighs social unrest and Bolshevism.

Stoddard writes as an outside observer of his own time, and his views carry the biases of that era. Even so, the book maps how Muslim peoples from North Africa to India faced empire, reform, and revolt after the First World War. Readers get a period survey of a world in rapid transition.
24314-mystics-and-saints-of-islam:
Claud Field wrote this study of Islamic mysticism, published in London by Francis Griffiths in 1910. Its chapters move from pantheistic Sufism through Hasan Basri, Rabia the woman Sufi, and Ibrahim ben Adham. Fudhayl ben Ayaz, Bayazid Bastami, Zu'n Nun of Egypt, Mansur Hallaj, and Habib Ajami follow. Avicenna, Al Ghazzali, Fariduddin Attar, Suhrawardy, Jalaluddin Rumi, Sharani the Egyptian, and Mullah Shah close the book.

Appendixes treat Mohammedan conversions, an exposition of Sufism, Christian elements in Mohammedan literature, and Christ in Mohammedan tradition. Field opens by noting that the moral law of Moses, Buddha, Confucius, and the Gospel agree across ages, and that mysticism takes God as feeling and conscience, not understanding alone. Readers get a clear early survey of Sufi saints.
24655-tinker-s-dam:
Joseph Tinker wrote this short science-fiction story, illustrated by Schoenherr. Its hero, Gyp, is woken while shaving by a call on the TV-phone, which his orders forbid before breakfast except for a national emergency. On the screen is George Kelly, Director of the FBI and Gyp's boss, telling him to hurry.

Tinker's title points to an old showman's trick: divert attention from the thing you are really doing. The story turns on misdirection, as its hero is pulled into a case where nothing is quite what it seems. Readers get a fast, witty tale of spies, showmanship, and a dam built on deception.
24991-aunt-amy-or-how-minnie-brown-learn:
Francis Forrester's 1853 story, published in Boston by Geo. C. Rand for 'My Uncle Toby's Library,' tells how Minnie Brown learned to be a sunbeam. Walking Rosedale's principal street, Minnie meets Arthur Ellerslie, who tells her a letter waits in the post office. Sure it comes from her aunt Amy, she skips to the window, receives it from the good-natured postmaster, and runs home nearly out of breath to find her mother in the parlor.

Later, a lady walks to the beach with Minnie while Mrs. Brown, unwell, stays behind. The broad, calm sea sparkles in the sun, and the splash of waves and hoarse murmur sound like music to the child. She remarks that the sea roars yet is very calm, and her aunt answers that this is old Ocean's mildest voice; in a storm he speaks in thunder. Shells and shoreline complete the gentle tale.
2504-some-cities-and-san-francisco-and-r:
Hubert Howe Bancroft, the historian of the Pacific coast, writes of cities and of San Francisco's rise from the ashes in Some Cities and San Francisco and Resurgam. The essays reflect on urban life, the earthquake and fire, and the city's rebirth, with Bancroft's booster pride and historical sweep. Resurgam, Latin for I shall rise again, gives the book its motto.

The volume captures San Francisco at a turning point, confident after disaster. Its period voice and civic pride charm as history. California readers will find a stirring record. Bancroft collected one of the great private libraries of western Americana.
25213-the-masters-and-their-music-a-seri:
W. S. B. Mathews's Masters and Their Music, published in Philadelphia in 1898, offers illustrative programs for clubs, classes, and private study. Mathews treats music as literature and leads students to the great masters who set the pace for all who followed.

Programs cover Bach, Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, Mendelssohn, Schumann, Chopin, Liszt, and Wagner, with biographical, aesthetic, and critical notes. Chopin's section stresses his melancholy melody, running right-hand work over a simple bass, and his polonaises, nocturnes, and ballads. The book suits listeners learning to hear style, not just tunes.
25254-notes-on-islam:
Notes on Islam, by Sir Ahmed Hussain, collected and edited by Khan Bahadur Hajee Khaja Muhammad Hussain, was printed at Hyderabad in 1922. The notes were first written in 1917 for four readers, and they present Islam as a faith of reason, unity, and practical duty.

Topics include the first chapter of the Quran, what religion is, what true Islam is, unity and union, moderation, and evolution. Hussain teaches that God is one, infinite, and unconditioned by time or place, seen by finite minds as Creator, Preserver, and Judge. An appendix urges Muslim reformation, and the book closes with a prayer.
25966-camp-fire-and-wigwam:
Edward S. Ellis tells a frontier tale of captives, trappers, and the Shawnee scout Deerfoot in Camp Fire and Wigwam, printed by Porter and Coates in 1885. Contents run from home and a doubtful enterprise to captors and captives, a journey south, an involuntary bath, two visitors, and a surprise. Signal fires, an Indian village, a mountain crest, and a war feast follow, with Deerfoot's woodcraft at the heart.

Jack praises Deerfoot as a man of charmed life, fired on often yet without so much as a scar, like Washington in battle. His serious mother shakes her head over her knitting and warns that such luck is unknown in this world, and Deerfoot may yet fall by knife or bullet. Ellis writes of camp fires, lodges, and forest trails with brisk, boyish vigor.
26473-the-arts-of-persia-other-countries:
This volume catalogues a special exhibition of the H. Kevorkian collection, shown on the entire third floor of the Anderson Galleries, 489 Park Avenue, New York, from April 22 to May 15, 1926. Its aim was to gather under one roof representative works from the many lands where Islam once held sway, across different epochs and stages of civilization. Visitors could study them with little waste of time.

Illustrated pieces include a painted stucco bas-relief excavated at Ray, ancient Rhages, dated before the twelfth century. The text traces a new artistic expression born from the fusion of Muhammadan doctrine with older Persian culture. It also points readers to permanent Near Eastern displays at the Metropolitan Museum, Boston's Museum of Fine Arts, and Philadelphia's University Museum.
26540-boy-scouts-in-the-canal-zone-or-th:
G. Harvey Ralphson published this boys' adventure novel in 1911. It sends his New York patrols to Panama with Lieutenant Gordon of the United States Secret Service. Patrol leader Ned Nestor and younger scouts such as Jimmie McGraw, Jack Bosworth, and Harry Stevens make the trip. Gordon suspects a plot to wreck the great Gatun Dam with explosives.

Jungle chases, a stolen emerald necklace, and hidden enemies tangle the dam plot with a second mystery. The scouts must sort which strangers belong to which scheme. Chapters move from the Gatun locks to ruined temples and night marches, ending with the tangle straightened out. It is a fast, patriotic serial of its era, built on teamwork, codes, and narrow escapes.
26981-pan-islam:
G. Wyman Bury's Pan-Islam, published by Macmillan in 1919, examines a force that the First World War had pushed into headlines. Bury warns at once that his book is not a religious treatise, but a study of a political and social movement.

Its chapters trace the idea's origin and meaning, its bearing on the war, and its strength and weakness against its great rival, the Christian Church. A chapter on Moslem and missionary closes with a plea for tolerance, arguing that a counterfeit jihad in Palestine and Syria shattered against good faith.
27697-the-mouse-and-the-moonbeam:
Eugene Field wrote this small fantasy, published in New York in 1919, copyrighted in 1912 by Charles Scribner's Sons, who permitted this small private edition. It tells what happened while a child slept, as the narrator saw and heard it.

A clock stands in the corner. A moonbeam floats idly on the floor. A little mauve mouse comes from the hole in the chimney corner to frisk and scamper in the light. She dances daintily, sometimes on two legs and sometimes on four, always very merrily. The old clock sighs that mice are different nowadays from the grave and dignified mice of the good old times, like Mistress Velvetpaw and Master Sniffwhisker. The little mouse asks why she should not be merry.
27838-a-bachelor-s-dream:
Mrs. Hungerford, writing as The Duchess, published A Bachelor's Dream with the Prudential Book Company of New York. It opens with Dr. Brudenell, a bachelor doctor, perplexed in his brougham on a Saturday evening in the Essex Road, unable to consult his excellent housekeeper Mrs. Jessop.

The doctor orders his coachman Patrick to drive to Petersham Villa instead of home, setting a romantic comedy in motion. Light, witty, and theatrical, the novel follows a confirmed bachelor toward love through misunderstandings, household comedy, and the social world of late Victorian London.
28069-alice-in-blunderland-an-iridescent:
John Kendrick Bangs wrote Alice in Blunderland in 1907 as a satire of municipal ownership, borrowing Lewis Carroll's Alice. Alice falls into Blunderland, a city where the government runs everything: trolleys that will not move, a gas plant, city police, and even a department of public verse. Albert Levering drew the pictures.

Chapters follow Alice through a municipal chewery and toothery, a Municipaphone, and the ownership of children, with the Cheshire Cat and March Hare in tow. Bangs turns Carroll's nonsense into jokes about city politics and reform. The book amuses readers who enjoy political satire dressed as a children's dream.
310-before-adam:
A modern man dreams in pictures of a life before men walked upright. Jack London's Before Adam, published in 1906, opens with a child tormented by dream pictures he never saw awake. The narrator learns he is different, a creature with an older memory.

His dreams recover a folk of tree dwellers, their fights, loves, and first steps on land. London frames the tale with evolution: from sea to trees to upright walking. The novel's eighteen chapters mix adventure with early science. It shows London's imagination at its strangest. London's dream device anticipates later tales of racial memory.
4294-tales-of-aztlan-the-romance-of-a-he:
George Hartmann wrote these tales to keep fresh the memory of Captain William Owen O'Neill, a hero of the Spanish-American War. The volume joins the romance of O'Neill with incidents from the life of a western pioneer and other tales, in a revised edition of 1908. A final tale, A Maid of Yavapai, honors Sharlot M. Hall, a noted Arizona pioneer.

The stories mix war memory with frontier life in Arizona, told by a writer close to the country. Hartmann's purpose is memorial as much as literary: to fix a hero's name and a pioneer's world before they fade. The book appeals to readers of Arizona history and of Spanish-American War remembrance.
4837-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
William the Silent's assassination opens this volume, and John Lothrop Motley measures what the Dutch lost with him. For nearly twenty years the prince had held the revolt together. His murder by a lone fanatic leaves Holland and Zealand facing Spain's vast power. A provisional council governs in his place, and his children carry his name forward.

The narrative then surveys the provinces. Holland and Zealand hold firm. Flanders weakens, and Ghent falls to Alexander Farnese's skill. Motley also traces the spread of Protestantism and the question of who should hold sovereignty next. The volume is both an obituary for a founder and an account of a republic forced to govern without him.
4838-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
After the death of William the Silent, the Dutch provinces must find new allies, and John Lothrop Motley traces how England weighed the risk of helping them. Queen Elizabeth and her ministers debate whether to face Spain, court France as a partner, and send an embassy to The Hague.

The narrative moves through council rooms and diplomatic letters, with Walsingham and Burghley pulling in different directions. It shows a small republic seeking protection without surrendering its freedom, and a queen reluctant to fund a war she feared. The result is a clear view of diplomacy as a slow, uneasy bargain.
4839-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
Antwerp's great siege takes shape in this volume, and John Lothrop Motley explains why the city mattered so much to both sides. Farnese prepares with care, drawing on William the Silent's foresight, while inside the walls Burgomaster Sainte Aldegonde struggles against anarchy, rival commanders, and opposition to Orange's plan.

Supplying Antwerp proves the hardest problem, since the patriots fail to pierce the dykes and Parma builds his bridge across the Scheldt. Motley follows the siege through correspondence as well as cannon fire, with Farnese writing to the citizens even as his guns close in. Readers see a rich trading city slowly cut off from the sea.
4840-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
In 1585, Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma, tries to strangle the Dutch revolt by seizing its ports and river crossings, and John Lothrop Motley follows the campaign in close detail. A surprise attack on Ostend collapses when Spanish troops break ranks to loot, and the citizens drive them out.

The fighting then shifts to Antwerp, where engineer Gianibelli's fire ships explode against Parma's bridge and patriots attack the Kowenstyn dyke. Motley balances siege craft, daring raids, and the despair of civilians caught between armies. It is a gripping chapter of a war decided as much by engineering and nerve as by pitched battle.
4841-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
Antwerp's surrender closes the siege begun in the previous volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the painful bargaining that ended it. Sainte Aldegonde, discouraged and trapped, negotiates with the enemy through Richardot, addresses the prince's deputies, and faces suspicion over his conduct as the net tightens.

Parma's private views, the city's commotion, and Marnix's oration all shape the capitulation, after which Alexander enters in triumph and rebuilds the citadel. Motley weighs Marnix's mistakes fairly, neither excusing nor condemning him outright. The volume captures the cost of losing the Netherlands' greatest port, and the arguments over blame that followed.
4842-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
During 1585, Dutch envoys cross to England to beg for help against Spain, and John Lothrop Motley follows their hard bargaining with Queen Elizabeth. The envoys meet Walsingham, Leicester, and the queen herself, offering guarantees while Elizabeth haggles over terms and refuses the sovereignty they offer.

Oldenbarnevelt emerges as a central figure, and the talks reveal England's weakness as well as its power. Motley presents diplomacy as theater and arithmetic at once: speeches at Greenwich, private audiences, and careful letters. Readers see how a republic and a monarchy negotiated an alliance neither side fully trusted.
4843-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
Sir John Norris's mission to Holland opens this volume, and John Lothrop Motley uses it to expose Elizabeth's parsimony toward her Dutch allies. Davison labors through long negotiations, vexed by the queen's caprice, while Count Maurice writes friendly letters and Louisa de Coligny adds her voice to the talks.

Leicester complains vehemently, the queen's manifesto tries to justify her course, and Sir Philip Sidney arrives at Flushing as a sign of English commitment. Motley shows an alliance held together by envoys' patience rather than royal generosity. Readers learn how much of early modern war depended on pay, promises, and the tempers of monarchs.
4844-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, lands in Holland in December 1585 as England's lieutenant general, and John Lothrop Motley charts his stormy reception. Cheered at Flushing and installed at The Hague, Leicester accepts the office of governor general, then collides with the queen who sent him.

Elizabeth's angry letters, Leicester's excuses, and missions back and forth to London fill the narrative, while English troops go unpaid and hungry. Motley also weighs Leicester's secret aims and his clashes with Dutch leaders. The volume is a study in how a grand gesture of alliance can unravel through pride, mistrust, and poor supply.
4845-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
Leicester's letters home fill this volume, and John Lothrop Motley shows how a commander's self-defense damaged the alliance he served. The earl excuses himself at Davison's expense, writes to Burghley, and watches suspicion spread through Holland as the queen's angry letters reach the States.

The States answer for their conduct, Leicester loses credit in Holland, and one well-timed letter briefly calms the queen, who then permits the authority she had granted. Motley follows her shifting moods, her attempts to mislead Walsingham, and her injustice to Heneage. The narrative is a close study of how court politics abroad could unravel a war effort.
4846-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
Secret talks between Parma and the English court dominate this 1586 volume, and John Lothrop Motley exposes a peace intrigue that nearly betrayed the Dutch cause. Agents Grafigni and Bodman carry offers between Farnese and Elizabeth's peace party, until Walsingham detects the plot and the schemers are baffled.

Meanwhile both armies starve through winter, Drake's victories unsettle Parma, and Leicester fumes at his treatment by London. Motley closes with Parma urging Philip to invade England outright. The volume reads like a spy story inside a war history, showing how back-channel diplomacy could matter as much as any siege.
4847-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
William the Silent's murder frames this volume, which John Lothrop Motley uses to survey the revolt at its darkest hour. The prince's assassination leaves the provinces without their guiding figure, and the narrative weighs the spread of Protestantism, Spain's vast power, and the religious roots of the rebellion.

Holland and Zealand hold firm under a provisional council, while Flanders weakens and Ghent falls to Alexander Farnese. Motley also follows William's children and the disposal of sovereignty after his death. Readers get both a portrait of the murdered leader and a map of a cause that had to survive him.
4873-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
A Dutch invasion of Flanders and the battle of Nieuport return in this volume, and John Lothrop Motley retells the campaign from its planning to its results. The States-General land troops on the Spanish coast, take Oudenburg and nearby places, and surprise Nieuport, before the archduke retakes the forts and traps the army in a dilemma.

The archduke's attack throws Count Ernest's cavalry into panic, yet the Dutch main force holds and defeats the Spanish army. Motley weighs the expedition's effect on the republic, which had acted defensively for years and now risked an offensive. The volume is a study in boldness: a gamble that proved Dutch arms abroad, at heavy cost.
4874-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
After the Nieuport campaign exhausts both armies, the war concentrates on Ostend, and John Lothrop Motley follows the long siege that became its center. Mutinous Spanish soldiers rampage in Hungary, Dunkirk pirates raid the coasts, and Maurice attacks Rheinberg while the archduke invests Ostend.

The narrative details the belligerents, the feigned offer by Sir Francis Vere to capitulate, and reinforcements arriving from the States. Motley weighs the general against the statesman, asking what sieges cost and what they gained. Readers see a war of attrition in which a single port could absorb years of effort from both sides.
4875-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
Ostend's protracted siege drags on in this volume, and John Lothrop Motley sets it beside Dutch ventures overseas. While Maurice marches again and besieges Grave, the archduke's army suffers a formidable mutiny, and a Portuguese expedition plants the first Batavian trading settlement on Java.

Jacob Heemskerk captures a Lisbon carrack, an embassy arrives from the King of Atsgen in Sumatra, and Frederic Spinola's privateer fleet is destroyed by English and Dutch cruisers. Grave surrenders, yet Ostend's siege continues through hurricane and hardship. Motley links a Flemish port's suffering to a republic becoming a trading empire.
4876-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
Elizabeth's death in 1603 changes the Dutch republic's world, and John Lothrop Motley follows the legations sent to her successor. James I unites England and Scotland, and the States' envoy seeks an audience while Henry IV of France sends De Rosny with his own mission and sharp opinions of the English.

De Rosny meets the States' envoy privately, presses his case at court, and hears hints from the Duke of Northumberland, while James promises to protect the Netherlands against Spain. Motley sketches the new king's character and the piracy, ceremony, and bargaining of a court in transition. The volume captures a republic renegotiating its place among monarchs.
4877-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
Maurice's Flemish campaign of 1604 centers on Sluys, and John Lothrop Motley follows the army from its landing to the town's capitulation. Fort St. Catharine's garrison flees, Ysendyke and Aardenburg surrender, and a skirmish at Stamper's Hook precedes the siege, which Spinola tries in vain to relieve.

Lewis Gunther of Nassau dies in the fighting, and at Ostend the exhausted garrison finally surrenders, leaving a scene of desolation after evacuation. Motley notes that the States-General had forgotten Nieuport's lesson about holding exposed places. The volume pairs a successful siege with a surrendered one, showing war as a ledger of gains and losses.
4878-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
The campaign of 1606 tests Maurice's standing, and John Lothrop Motley follows a year of maneuver, weather, and mutiny. Spinola pushes for the Waal and Yssel. He takes Lochem and Rheinberg and besieges Groll. Maurice wins Lochem back, but his try to retake Groll fails when the foe appears without warning.

Around the fighting, the pope quarrels with Venice. Du Terrail surprises Sluys. Catholic troops mutiny. Motley notes how rain and season shaped operations as surely as generalship. The volume closes with the war of independence winding down, its great sieges giving way to the politics of peace.
4879-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
A Dutch fleet under Heemskerk sails for Spain and Portugal in this volume, and John Lothrop Motley narrates a sea fight in which both commanders die. The States-General, stung by an earlier check off Spain, send Heemskerk against the Spanish war fleet under D'Avila, and the Dutch win the encounter at the cost of their admiral's life.

Motley recalls Klaaszoon's self-devotion in the earlier crisis, which had shown that Dutch fleets needed only skilled handling and determined leaders to beat their enemy in western seas. The narrative honors seamanship and sacrifice without romanticizing them. Readers get a compact naval action that restored a republic's confidence at sea.
4880-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
Peace deliberations in Spain open this volume, and John Lothrop Motley shows a project few wanted and many feared. Courtiers grow disaffected, complaints pile against Spinola, and Henry IV weighs his stance toward the republic while James of England wishes the States restored to Spain.

French commissioners arrive, President Jeannin addresses the States-General, and the dangers of a truce are debated in public. Philip's ratification reaches The Hague through Verreyken, the Spanish treaty is rejected, and the Dutch fleet withdraws from the Peninsula. Motley traces a negotiation that failed, and why its failure mattered to every court in Europe.
4881-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
Truce negotiations take over from open war in this volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows Spinola's reception at The Hague and his meeting with Maurice. The republic signs a treaty with France, Spanish commissioners appear before the States-General, and stormy discussions expose Spain's real object in talking peace.

The India trade becomes a sticking point, the peace project is abandoned, and talks turn to a truce, with an armistice prolonged through further delays. A treaty with England follows, while Friar Neyen carries proposals to Spain and Philip procrastinates over conditions. Motley shows negotiation as warfare by other means, with every clause contested.
4882-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
A proposed truce between the States and Spain divides the republic in this volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the faction fight it ignites. Maurice works to counter Barneveld's designs, popular feeling turns against the advocate, and Spanish commissioners return, trifle, and are finally dismissed.

The accidental discovery of the archdukes' secret instructions sharpens the debate, and President Jeannin compares the Dutch and Swiss republics in an oration before the States-General. Motley also notes the marriage project joining France and Spain. The volume shows a young republic arguing over peace itself: whether a truce would save it or sell it.
4883-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
The Twelve Years' Truce is signed in this volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the talks from groundwork to ratification. Plenipotentiaries arrange the terms, the States-General, the archdukes, and the King of Spain all ratify, and the negotiations close after years of war.

President Jeannin appeals for Catholics, and Motley treats religious liberty as the war's true fruit, even as internal arrangements under peace take shape. The deaths of John, Duke of Cleves, and Jacob Arminius lead into theological warfare between Arminius's and Gomarus's doctrines. The volume ends a long war with a truce, and opens a new quarrel over belief that would soon divide the republic itself.
4884-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
The battle of Nieuport in 1600 anchors this volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the States' bold invasion of Flanders. Dutch troops land on the Spanish coast, capture Oudenburg and other places, and surprise Nieuport, only to see the archduke retake the forts and throw the army into a dilemma.

Count Ernest's cavalry panics and breaks, yet the main army rallies and defeats the Spanish force in a hard-fought action whose details Motley sets out carefully. Mutiny in the Spanish ranks and the state of the archdukes' provinces form the background. The volume shows a republic willing to invade, and the battle that proved it could.
4885-history-of-the-united-netherlands-f:
William the Silent's assassination is the starting point for this Motley volume, which surveys a revolt suddenly deprived of its leader. The narrative asks what held the provinces together after nearly twenty years under one man's expanding character, and how Spain's power and the religious roots of the rising shaped the answer.

Holland and Zealand answer with courage under a provisional council, while Flanders falters and Ghent falls to Farnese's adroitness. William's children and the question of sovereignty run through the account. The volume serves as both a tribute to the murdered prince and a sober audit of the cause he left behind.
5335-raspberry-jam:
Carolyn Wells's Raspberry Jam is a detective novel featuring Fleming Stone, opening with a dispute over telepathy and mind reading. Aunt Abby insists there is something in mind reading, while Eunice warns that if she keeps on, she may say what she thinks. The argument sets the tone for a mystery of séances and mediums.

Chapters follow the great Hanlon, a trip to Newark, a stunt, the Emburys, a slammed door, a vision. Marigny the medium appears, as Stone sorts truth from trickery. Readers get a lively period mystery, with Wells's usual mix of humour, suspects. The detective trusts evidence over the supernatural.
6363-life-is-a-dream:
Denis Florence Mac-Carthy translates Calderon's dramas fully from Spanish in the metre of the original, in an 1873 London volume from Henry S. King. Two dramas here are Calderon's most celebrated, and the first, La Vida es Sueno, has been played with success on almost every European stage except England's. In Moscow in the winter of 1866 to 1867 it drew crowded houses, and in Stockholm a queen expired in the theatre during its performance.

Mac-Carthy's introduction calls the play much studied in England for literary value and lyrical beauty, even where it was not staged. Clorilene bears a son under prodigies of heaven, and the verse that follows, in Mac-Carthy's metre, tells of fate, knowledge, and a man injured by what he knows. The book gives English readers Calderon as poetry, not only as plot, in a translation that keeps his music.
7491-de-amicitia-scipio-s-dream:
Cicero's De Amicitia, On Friendship, is one of the great short works of Roman philosophy, and this volume pairs it with Scipio's Dream. Laelius, famed for wisdom, speaks after the death of his friend Scipio, consoling himself with faith in immortality and with the wish that their friendship be remembered forever. True friendship, he argues, can exist only among good men, and it is founded not on need but on nature.

The synopsis lists the essay's themes: truth-telling even when it offends, the arts of flattery, and virtue as the soul of friendship. Scipio's Dream adds a cosmic vision, in which Scipio visits his ancestor and sees the earth from above. Andrew P. Peabody's translation, with introduction and notes, makes both works open to modern readers.
869-the-soul-of-nicholas-snyders-or-the-:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this tale of Nicholas Snyders, the miser of Zaandam, and the fate of his soul. Snyders hoards his gold in a Dutch town, counting each coin while life passes him by, until a reckoning comes that money cannot buy off. The story, published in 1908, wears its moral lightly.

Jerome blends folk-tale dread with his usual humour, letting the miser's greed speak for itself. The tale asks what a life spent gathering is worth when the gathering ends. It stands as a neat, dark fable among Jerome's lighter pieces, and a warning against letting wealth harden the heart.
8734-east-of-paris-sketches-in-the-ga-ti:
Miss Betham-Edwards sketches the country east of Paris, through the Gatinais, Bourbonnais, and Champagne, town by town. Melun, Moret-sur-Loing, Bourron, Larchant, Recloses, and Nemours open the route, followed by La Charite-sur-Loire, Pougues, Nevers, Moulins, Souvigny, and Sens. Later chapters reach Arcis-sur-Aube, Rheims, Soulaines, Bar-sur-Aube, St Jean de Losne, and Nancy, before crossing into Germanised Lorraine and Alsace.

Betham-Edwards, a seasoned English traveller in France, writes with a novelist's eye for streets, inns, churches, and local character. Her sketches blend history, anecdote, and personal encounter, at a time when Alsace-Lorraine's fate was fresh news. Readers planning a French journey, or simply armchair travelling, get a leisurely, well-informed companion to a region less visited than Paris or Provence.
954-tom-swift-and-his-war-tank-or-doing-:
Tom Swift does his bit for Uncle Sam in this wartime tale by Victor Appleton, building a war tank for the army. Past memories, Tom's indifference, and Ned's worry open the story, while queer doings and the taunt of slacker spur Tom to work. Detective Rad and a night test put the tank through its paces.

The tank, a runaway giant that bridges gaps and crushes wire, proves its worth in trials that mimic battle. Appleton writes with patriotic energy, praising invention in service of country. The book is a lively Tom Swift war story, from the years when tanks were new and boys followed the war in the papers.
962-the-poems-of-henry-kendall-with-biog:
Henry Kendall wrote these poems of Australia, gathered here with a biographical note by Bertram Stevens. Kendall, a native-born Australian poet who lived from 1841 to 1882, sang of bush, sea, and mountain, and of the sorrows and hopes of colonial life. The edition breaks long lines by metre, as the note explains.

Kendall's verse is musical and melancholy, rooted in the Australian landscape he loved. His best poems, on rivers, forests, and lost friends, made him his country's first notable poet. The volume preserves his work for readers who want the voice of early Australia, tender, lyrical, and haunted by distance.
a-midsummer-night-s-dream:
William Shakespeare's comedy moves between the court of Athens and a wood where fairies rule the night. This text keeps the old spelling of the early printed editions, as the editor's notes explain. Duke Theseus prepares to marry Hippolyta while young lovers Hermia, Lysander, Helena, and Demetrius quarrel over who must wed whom.

In the wood, Oberon and Titania fight over a changeling boy, and Puck's love juice sends every heart after the wrong person. A group of workmen rehearse a sad play about Pyramus and Thisbe and perform it badly and sweetly at the wedding. Dawn sorts the lovers into pairs, and Puck asks the audience's pardon.
anglo-saxon-chronicle-giles-ingram:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is a set of annals kept in Old English at monasteries across England, here in J. A. Giles's translation as revised by James Ingram. The entries run from the Roman invasion to the Norman Conquest and beyond. Monks added year by year, sometimes in a line, sometimes in a small epic.

Battles, kings, comets, famines, and Viking fleets pass in terse sequence. The annal for Cynewulf and Cyneheard breaks into a full tale of loyalty and revenge. Alfred's wars, the martyrdom of archbishops, and the coming of William the Conqueror all stand in their keepers' own words. The Chronicle is England's diary of itself for six hundred years.
before-adam:
Jack London wrote Before Adam, published in book form in 1907 after running as a serial. Its narrator is a modern man troubled since childhood by dreams so real they feel like memories: memories of a life lived before Adam, in a cave-dwelling folk of the Middle Pleistocene. In dreams he is Big-Tooth, a young male of the Folk, growing up among tree nests, water holes, and constant fear.

Big-Tooth's world holds the gentle Folk, the more advanced Fire People with their bows, and the brute Red-Eye, whose killings haunt the tale. London builds the story on the idea that racial memory can pass down the ages. The result is part adventure, part meditation on how far humankind has, and has not, come.
boy-scouts-in-mexico-or-on-guard-with-un:
G. Harvey Ralphson, writing as a scout master, sent his boy patrols to the Mexican border in Boy Scouts in Mexico. The young scouts go by patrol names, Wolf, Black Bear, and Panther, and their vacation turns into border duty with Uncle Sam. Chapters promise signals on the mountain, a strange disappearance, captures, mistaken arrests, and a crime whose story comes out near the end.

Ralphson packs in woodcraft, codes, and patriotic instruction, dedicating the book to American boys and girls in hopes of usefulness and self-reliance. The plot runs through renegades and underground finds toward the Canal Zone. It is early scout fiction at full gallop: earnest, breathless, and sure that a trained boy is a match for any smuggler.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-st-e:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on St. Emmeram describes a Benedictine house at Regensburg, named for the city's patron saint, its famed founder. St. Emmeram lived in the mid-seventh century, and 652 stands as the likely date of the house's start.

Its roots lay in a chapel holding much-loved relics, made larger in 697 by Theodo, Duke of Bavaria, who built a new Benedictine house with Apollonius as first abbot. Charlemagne made it larger still about 800, with wide lands and many rights. When St. Boniface split Bavaria into four sees in 739, Regensburg's first bishop set his seat at St. Emmeram, later moving it to St. Stephen's beside the present church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abel-son-of-a:
Abel was the second son of Adam, and this entry weighs what his name may mean, from vanity and shortness of life to sorrow, lamentation, or shepherd. Cain, the firstborn, farmed the soil, while Abel kept flocks, so the brothers were linked by birth and by work. Abel appears in the Old Testament only in Genesis 4, and St. Augustine reads him as a type of the regenerate man, set against Cain as the natural man.

Nothing is said of Abel's descendants, so the entry supposes he left none alive at the birth of Seth. It also covers the Abelians, a North African sect named by Augustine who claimed to imitate Abel by marrying yet refusing marital relations. Legends about Cain and Abel from the Bible, the Koran, and the Talmud close the piece, with sources for readers who want the fuller tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham:
Abraham, first called Abram, is the patriarch whose story fills Genesis 11:26 to 25:18. This entry opens with a brief outline of that life before discussing him from several angles. Thare took Abram, his wife Sarai, and Lot from Ur of the Chaldees to Haran. After Thare's death Abram obeyed God's call into Chanaan, building altars at Sichem and Bethel. A famine drove him to Egypt, where fear for his life led him to pass Sarai off as his sister.

Beyond the outline, the entry treats Abraham in the Old Testament, in the New Testament, in profane history, and in legend. It weighs the meaning of his name, from lofty father to a dialect form of Abram. It also deals with the composite character of the Genesis narrative, joining older collections with a later priestly one. Readers get both the patriarch's story and the scholarship that surrounds it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam:
Adam is the first man and father of the human race, and this long entry starts with the etymology of the Hebrew adam. The word was probably first a common noun rather than a proper name. Semitic scholars diverge on its sense, and no theory fully satisfies. The root for man or mankind appears in only some Semitic tongues, as a native term only in Phoenician, Sabean, and probably Assyrian.

Genesis 2:7 links the name with ha-adamah, the ground, making man earthborn, as Latin homo is kin to humus. That ground etymology, though defended by some, is now generally abandoned. Others read the root as to be red, a sense it bears in Old Testament passages and in Arabic and Ethiopic. Beyond etymology the entry follows Adam through Genesis, the New Testament, and the legends around him, pointing readers to the Jewish Encyclopedia and Smith and Wace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adullam:
Adullam, Hebrew Adhullam and Vulgate Odollam, names both a Chanaanite city and a cave. The city stood west of Bethlehem at the foot of Juda's mountains. From Chanaanite hands it passed to Juda, was fortified by Roboam, was mentioned by the prophet Micheas, and after the exile was repeopled by Jews.

The Cave of Adullam sheltered David and his followers, as 1 Samuel 22 records. Some place it six miles southeast of Bethlehem in Wady Khareitun, but more probably it lies near the city of Adullam itself. The entry cites Clermont-Ganneau and Conder in the Palestine Exploration Fund memoirs and Muir in Hastings's Bible dictionary for readers tracing city and cave.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aelfric-abbot:
Aelfric, Abbot of Eynsham, also called the Grammarian, was author of the Anglo-Saxon homilies, a translator of scripture, and a writer on many miscellaneous subjects; born about 955, he died about 1020. His identity has drawn much controversy, and Freeman's Norman Conquest wrongly identifies him with Aelfric, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Of late years nearly all scholars have accepted Lingard and Dietrich's view that Anglo-Saxon literature knows but one famous Aelfric, who rose no higher than abbot. A monk of Winchester's Old Monastery under St. Athelwold, whose life he wrote in Latin, he was sent after ordination to Cerne Abbey in Dorset, then became abbot of newly founded Eynsham near Oxford in 1005. Most prolific of preserved Anglo-Saxon writers, he is remembered above all for his Homilies, around whose Eucharistic teaching a great controversy raged.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ahicam: Ahicam, a name meaning my brother has risen, served at Josias's high court and under both his two sons, shielding Jeremias from the angry populace's deadly fury. Saphan the scribe was his father; his son Godolias later governed the country under Nabuchodonosor. Scripture names him three times: 2 Kings 22:12, Jeremiah 26:24, Jeremiah 40:5.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alan-of-walsi:
Alan of Walsingham died about 1364. A celebrated architect, he first appears in 1314, a junior monk at Ely noted for skill in goldsmith's work and acquaintance with mechanics' principles. In 1331, when sub-prior, he designed and began the cathedral's St. Mary's Chapel, now Trinity Church.

December 1321 saw him elected sacristan, with sole charge of the cathedral fabric. In February 1322 the great tower fell, carrying the choir and attached portions with it. Instead of rebuilding the four piers of the Norman square tower, Alan pushed the supports a bay into each arm of the cross. So he spread the weight on eight piers instead of four and gained a magnificent central octagonal hall, domed with a lofty lantern. The result was beautiful and in every sense original. Alan almost certainly never travelled beyond his convent, knowing domed Eastern churches only by hearsay.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-of-:
Alexander of Neckam, also called Necham, was an English scholar born in Hertfordshire in 1157 and dead at Kempsey in Worcestershire in 1217. He studied at the abbey school of St. Albans and then at Paris, in the school of Petit Pons. In 1180 he began teaching with success, drawing many students by his broad knowledge and his Latin style in prose and verse.

Returning to England in 1186, Neckam taught at Dunstable and then at St. Albans. He joined the Augustinians and was chosen Abbot of Cirencester in 1213. He wrote prolifically: a grammar, commentaries on Scripture and Aristotle, theological treatises, sermons, and a verse translation of Aesop's Fables. But most of his works remain in manuscript. Only two have been printed: On the Natures of Things, covering heavens, stars, air, earth, water, and life, and the poem In Praise of Divine Wisdom. He is the first European author to mention the mariner's compass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amsterdam:
Amsterdam, capital and second residential city of the Netherlands, lies in a semicircle on the Ij at the mouth of the Amstel. It is joined to the North Sea by a canal built between 1865 and 1879. Its story starts in 1204, when Gijsbrecht II, Lord of the Amstel, built a fortress here. The settlement won city rank in 1301, then grew rich on merchants from Brabant and Flanders.

By the end of the fifteenth century more than twenty monasteries stood in the city, though only the Beguinage kept its old form through the Reformation. Pilgrims crowded the Holy Room, scene of the Miracle of Amsterdam, reached by the street still called the Holy Way. After full religious liberty came in 1848 and the hierarchy returned in 1853, Amsterdam became a deanery under Haarlem with eighteen Catholic parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-frede:
Antoine-Frederic Ozanam, a French scholar born at Milan in 1813, joined learning to charity. At eighteen he defended the faith in print, then studied law in Paris, where doubt shook him until a priest teacher restored his belief. He vowed to serve the truth that had given him peace, and he kept that vow for life.

At twenty, with seven friends, he founded the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul, to back faith with works of charity. His Dante thesis won his doctorate, and he rose to the Sorbonne chair in foreign literature in 1844. His books, praised for warmth and exactness, remain readable introductions to their subjects, and he spread his charity society with tireless zeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assam:
Assam is a prefecture apostolic in the Calcutta church province in India, established in 1889 and staffed by the Society of the Divine Saviour. Its mother house stands at Rome, with priests resident at Shillong. Assam covers the civil province of Assam, with Bhutan and Manipur. Its native population runs to 7,000,000, while Catholics number 1,800, served by six secular and ten regular priests.

Chapels stand at Shillong, Gauhati, Bondashill, Railing, Laitkinsew, Silchar, Cherrapunji, Lamin, and elsewhere, twenty-five chapels and nineteen stations in all. The mission also runs fifteen elementary schools with 300 pupils, two orphanages under Sisters of the Divine Saviour, four charitable dispensaries, and one asylum for aged women. It also runs a small hospital at Shillong, while seventeen non-Catholic sects count 18,000 adherents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balaam:
Balaam, son of Beor of Pethor, is the seer Balak, King of Moab, hired to curse Israel. His story runs through Numbers 22 to 24, with echoes in Deuteronomy, Joshua, Nehemiah, Micah, Peter, Jude, and Revelation. His name's derivation is uncertain, though Neubauer links it to a god called Ammo or Ammi. Balak, alarmed at Israel's victories over the Amorites, sent messengers with presents to fetch him.

Men then prized a curse highly, and Balaam held special repute: whom he blessed was blessed, and whom he cursed was cursed. He first consulted the Lord and was refused leave to go, so he sent the embassy away. A second, grander embassy won leave on condition that he speak only what God commanded. Critics date his fourth prophecy no earlier than David's reign, noting later retouching of such writings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balsam:
Balsam is an oily, resinous, scented substance that flows from certain plants, by itself or by cutting. The Church mixes it with olive oil to make chrism. True balsams include the costly Balm of Gilead, or Mecca, grown in Arabia, Egypt, and Syria. Copaiva balsam and those of Peru and Tolu come chiefly from South America.

Church use of balsam is very ancient, reaching back perhaps to Apostolic times. Scarcity and price have left the Latin Church content with balm alone in holy chrism. In the East, where the climate suits such plants, the Church uses thirty-six precious perfumes in the oil. The Latin Church fixes neither amount nor quality: enough to scent the oil suffices. The mingling is meant as an outward sign of the good odor of Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bedlam:
Bedlam is the popular shortening of Bethlehem, Hebrew for house of bread, a London hospital founded in 1247 as a priory in Bishopsgate Street. Simon Fitz Mary founded it for the order of St Mary of Bethlehem, to serve the poor sick and homeless. By the fourteenth century it partly housed the insane, as a 1405 Royal Commission report shows. In 1375 it became a royal hospital, seized as an alleged alien priory, and later reverted to the city.

By Tyndale's day the word meant a madman, and in 1547 Henry VIII granted Bedlam with St Bartholomew's to London. A new hospital rose at Finsbury Circus in 1674, and the old site now holds Liverpool Street station. Hogarth pictured fashionable ladies visiting it as a show, and after an 1851 investigation it came under regular inspection. It now houses about three hundred patients with over sixty attendants, curing more than half each year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-birmingham:
Birmingham, an English diocese, receives a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. One of thirteen dioceses restored by Pius IX in 1850, it covers Oxford, Stafford, Warwick, and Worcester, taking its name from Birmingham, the largest town of the four counties. Before 1850 the same counties lay in the Midland, then Central, vicariate, ruled by vicars-apostolic since 1688.

Bishop Milner, learned in controversy, was its most illustrious vicar, and William Bernard Ullathorne became its first bishop, enthroned at St. Chad's in 1850 with Newman preaching. Oscott College, home to converts, anchors its story. The entry joins restoration history to a working diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-thomas-cot:
Blessed Thomas Cottam, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Lancashire in 1549 to Protestant parents, he was executed at Tyburn in 1582. After Brasenose College, Oxford, and a London grammar-school mastership, Thomas Pound converted him, and he went to Douai, ordained deacon at Cambrai in 1577.

Hoping for the Indian mission, he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Rome in 1579, but fever sent him to Lyons and then Reims, where he joined the English mission instead. Arrested on landing, he was racked and tried with Campion's companions. The entry presents a convert whose mission changed from India to England's scaffold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-josep:
An encyclopedia life of Charles Joseph Kickham, Irish patriot, novelist, and poet from County Tipperary. Born in 1828, he lost much of his sight and hearing as a boy when a flask of damp gunpowder exploded while he dried it. He joined the Young Ireland rising of 1848, then the Fenians, a secret movement for Irish independence, and helped edit their paper, The Irish People, until his arrest in 1865.

Sentenced to fourteen years of penal servitude, a harsh prison punishment, Kickham's health broke down, and he was freed in 1869 nearly blind. He then turned wholly to writing, producing novels of rural Irish life, above all Knocknagow, published in 1879 and praised as a faithful portrait of a Tipperary village. His fiction blends humour and pathos, a tender sadness, with close observation of small farmers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chatham:
A history of the Diocese of Chatham, which covers the northern half of New Brunswick in Canada. The land once belonged to the Diocese of Quebec, then to St. John, until St. John was divided on 8 May 1860 and Chatham was created. James Rogers, consecrated in August of that year, arrived to find only seven priests for a vast country, much of it French Acadian.

Rogers ruled for forty-two years and left a diocese of forty-seven parishes and fifty-one priests when he resigned in 1902. His successor, Thomas Francis Barry, and the diocese then counted fifty-seven churches with resident priests and twenty-five missions, serving about 66,000 Catholics. Its schools included a classical college at Caraquet run by the Eudist Fathers, eight parish schools, and three schools taught by sisters. Two orphan asylums and four hospitals served the diocese, among them, Tracadie's government hospital for lepers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominic-schra:
Dominic Schram was a Benedictine theologian and canonist born at Bamberg on 24 October 1722. He took vows at Banz in 1743 and was ordained in 1748, then taught at his monastery in turn mathematics, canon law, philosophy, and theology. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he reluctantly became prior of Michelsberg at Bamberg in 1782 and returned to Banz five years later.

His chief works are a scientific compendium of dogmatic, scholastic, and moral theology in three volumes and an Institutions of Mystical Theology in two, judged his best. An analysis of the fathers and church writers ran to eighteen volumes, and he reworked Carranza's Summa of councils up to Pius the Sixth. He died at Banz in 1797.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-strans:
Edward Stransham was an English priest and martyr born at Oxford about 1554 and put to death at Tyburn in 1586. He took his degree at Saint John's College, Oxford, in 1575 or 1576, reached Douai in 1577, and moved with the college to Reims in 1578. Illness sent him home, but he returned to Reims in 1579 and was ordained at Soissons in December 1580.

He came back to England in June 1581 with his fellow martyr Nicholas Woodfen. In 1583 he returned to Reims with twelve Oxford converts, then spent about eighteen months at Paris near death from consumption. Arrested in Bishopsgate Street in London in July 1585 while saying Mass, he was condemned at the next assizes for being a priest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-haymo-of-fave:
Kent Franciscan Haymo of Faversham, a famed Paris lecturer and preacher before joining the Friars Minor about 1224, became one of the order's great reformers. As custos at Paris he helped carry the chapter's questions to Gregory IX, winning the bull Quo elongati of 1230. He later lectured at Oxford, Tours, Bologna, and Padua and negotiated reunion at Constantinople in 1233.

His revision of the Roman Curia's Breviary, published in 1241, grew into the Breviary of the whole Church. As general after Elias's deposition in 1239 he cut the provinces from seventy-two and barred lay brothers from superiors' posts where priests were available. He set friars to farming so they need not beg. He died at Anagni in 1243, praised on his tomb as England's highest glory among the Minors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-nutcomb:
Henry Nutcombe Oxenham, an English poet and controversialist, born at Harrow in 1829, studied at Harrow School and Balliol College, Oxford, and served as Anglican curate at Worminghall and St. Bartholomew's, Cripplegate, where Cardinal Manning received him into the Catholic Church. He entered St. Edmund's College intending priesthood, but left after minor orders, believing Anglican orders valid and himself already a priest, and spent the rest of his life in that anomalous position.

Oxenham's ambition was reunion of the Anglican and Catholic churches, pursued in a sympathetic reply to Pusey's Eirenicon and in his Lectures on Reunion of 1872. After the Vatican Council his unwillingness to accept papal infallibility, influenced by Döllinger, made his position stranger still. Yet he never outwardly broke with Rome and died in 1888 having received the sacraments from Father Lockhart. He also translated Döllinger's First Age of Christianity and wrote Catholic Eschatology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herbert-of-bo:
Herbert of Bosham, a biographer of St. Thomas Becket, was probably of Bosham in Sussex; his birth and death dates unknown. He joined Becket's household before 1162, when the new archbishop at once gave him a post advising on duties and directing scriptural studies. He stayed close to Thomas through episcopacy and exile to the very eve of the murder in Canterbury Cathedral. He proved the king and the royal customs' keenest antagonist, ready to beard Henry II.

After the martyrdom Herbert lived mainly on the Continent, complaining of neglect, and nothing is known of him after 1189. As biographer he enjoyed advantages as eyewitness, present at the trial at Northampton. He did not write until 1184, and his reminiscences are doubted for accuracy and exaggerating his own influence. His Life is therefore less valuable than Fitzstephen's, and extremely verbose, alongside a Liber Melorum in the martyr's praise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ihs-monogram:
IHS shortens the name of Jesus Christ. Christians were already shortening the Saviour's names in inscriptions by the third century, writing IH and XP for Jesus and Christus. A century later the chi-rho sigla served as more than shorthand: it worked as a symbol too.

Yet from the start, contraction was the usual method for sacred names, giving IHS and XPS, or IC and XC, for Iesous Christos. Latin writers kept these Greek contractions through the Middle Ages. In time people forgot what they meant, and misreading IHS produced the faulty spelling Jhesus. After the twelfth century the monogram spread further, as Bernard urged devotion to the Holy Name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-in-commendam:
In commendam is canon-law language for one way of granting a Church benefice. Commendam itself is the accusative of commenda, a Low Latin word for trust or custody, from commendare, to entrust. At first the phrase covered a stopgap grant: a benefice with no holder yet was put in someone's care for a time.

That stood against in titulum, the normal grant without conditions. Handing out benefices this way goes back to the fourth century. Ambrose, while Bishop of Milan, mentions a church he entrusted to someone until it gained its own bishop. Orléans' Third Council in 538 placed such grants under bishops' oversight, and Gregory the Great often gave churches and monasteries this way to bishops forced from their sees by barbarian invaders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-ozana:
French mathematician Jacques Ozanam was born at Bouligneux in 1640. He died at Paris on 3 April 1717. He came from a rich family that had left Judaism for Catholicism. The better known Antoine-Frédéric Ozanam sprang from the same family. Jacques began theology to please his father. But mathematics attracted him more strongly, and he mastered it without a teacher. At fifteen he produced a mathematical treatise.

After his father's death, he quit theology after four years of study. At Lyons he began giving free private lessons in mathematics. Later, when family property passed wholly to his elder brother, he reluctantly accepted fees. In 1670 he published trigonometric and logarithmic tables more accurate than those of Ulacq, Pitiscus, and Briggs. Lending money kindly to two strangers won him notice from a patron. The entry presents a self-taught mathematician of the age of Louis XIV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeroboam:
Jeroboam is the name of two kings of Israel, and this entry begins with the first, founder of the northern kingdom after the ten tribes broke away. Son of Nebat, an Ephraimite, he rose young under Solomon, overseeing forced labour for Ephraim and Manasseh on Jerusalem's Millo fortress and other works.

Seeing discontent under Solomon's extravagance, Jeroboam heard the prophet Ahijah promise him ten tribes if he stayed faithful. Impatient, he rebelled early, fled to Egypt's King Shishak, and returned after Solomon's death to lead the plea for lighter burdens. Rehoboam's harsh refusal split the kingdom, and Jeroboam took the northern crown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-adam:
